---
title: Outbound agents, actors inside
description: "How an Arkitekt app runs: an agent that dials out to the server and never opens a port, actors that run each action's tasks one at a time or in parallel, and agent-wide locks taken in a fixed order so devices are never commanded twice and never deadlock."
type: concept
---

When you call `run(app)`, your process becomes an **agent**. It connects to the server, says what
it offers, and runs the tasks it is handed. Two patterns shape how it does that: how it talks to
the outside, and how it runs work inside.

## Outbound only

An agent **dials out**. It opens one WebSocket to the server and keeps it open. It never listens on
a port, needs no public address and no firewall rule. Tasks reach it over the connection it opened.

This is the **reverse connection** (or pull) pattern used by CI runners and remote agents: the
worker connects to the coordinator, not the other way round. It is why the same app runs unchanged
on a laptop, behind a lab firewall, in a container and on a microcontroller, and why a deployment
never needs to know where its agents are.

When the connection drops, the agent reconnects with backoff and resends from its journal whatever
the server has not acknowledged. Running tasks follow their [disconnect
policy](/docs/build/python#disconnect-policy): keep going, or stop after a grace period.

## Actors inside

Inside the agent, each action is run by an **actor**: the thing that receives that action's
assignments and runs them. By default an actor is **serial**: tasks of the same action run one
after the other, in order. With `concurrency="parallel"` they may overlap.

This is the **actor model**, used loosely: each actor owns its own queue, and actors of one agent
run independently of each other. A slow "acquire" does not hold up a quick "read temperature".

## Locks across actors

Some things are shared between actions: the stage that both `move_to` and `autofocus` drive.
**Locks** say so. A state can name locks (`required_locks=`) that every action taking it holds, and
an action can name more (`locks=`). A task waits until it holds all of its locks, and releases them
when it ends.

Locks are agent-wide and are always taken **in the same global order**, so two tasks that need
overlapping locks cannot deadlock each other, whatever order their actions declared them in. A
lock is only held while a task actually runs, never while it waits in its actor's queue.

## What it buys

- **Runs anywhere.** No inbound connectivity, so no network configuration per lab.
- **Safe defaults for hardware.** Serial actors and locks mean one command at a time to a device,
  without writing any synchronization yourself.
- **Isolation between actions.** A long task blocks only its own action, and only if it is serial.

## What it costs

- **Serial is slower.** A computation that could run many times at once has to say
  `concurrency="parallel"`.
- **Locks are not re-entrant.** A task holding a lock that calls, directly or through a
  dependency, another action on the same agent that needs the same lock will wait for itself.
- **One connection to rule them all.** If the link to the server is down, the agent can do nothing
  new. Work in flight continues according to its disconnect policy and is reported later.
